text: Professional standard of care. A health practitioner must perform duties with the accuracy and honesty the profession requires, follow recognised scientific and technical standards, give the patient due care and comply with applicable laws. Quote: "must perform the duties of his job with the level of accuracy and honesty as required by the profession". Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 3.

metadata.themes: standard of care, duty of care, clinical protocols

text: Practise within grade and specialisation. The physician must follow the rules, systems and procedures for practising the profession according to grade and specialisation. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 4(1).

Record the patient's condition and history before diagnosis and treatment. Before diagnosis and treatment the physician must record the patient's health condition and personal and family medical history. MEDIMCOM uses this as the legal basis for requiring allergies, current treatments and pregnancy status before a prescription is cleared. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 4(2).

metadata.themes: medical history, mandatory information, allergies, pregnancy, current treatments

text: Use the diagnosis and treatment methods the condition requires. The physician must use the diagnostic and treatment methods required by the patient's condition. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 4(3).

Inform the patient of treatment options. The physician must keep the patient informed of the available treatment options. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 4(5).

metadata.themes: patient information, treatment options, informed consent

text: Written prescription with dose and usage. The physician must prescribe the medicine, its dose and method of use in writing, with the physician's name, signature and date, and explain the importance of the treatment to the patient or family. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 4(6).

metadata.themes: prescription, dose, posology, written prescription, signature, human prescriber

text: Inform the patient about the nature and seriousness of the condition. The physician must inform the patient of the nature and seriousness of the condition unless this would harm the patient or the patient cannot cope psychologically; family is informed when the patient lacks capacity or cannot be told. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 4(7).

metadata.themes: patient information, diagnosis disclosure, accessible communication

text: Inform about complications before intervention. Before an intervention the physician must inform the patient or family of possible complications, and identify and treat complications where possible. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 4(8).

No treatment without consent, except emergencies. Treating a patient without consent is prohibited, except where emergency intervention is required and consent cannot be obtained, or where the disease is infectious or threatens public health or safety. Quote: "Treat a patient without his consent except in the cases requiring emergent medical intervention". Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 5(1).

metadata.themes: consent, informed consent, emergency exception, infectious disease

text: No prescription before clinical examination; distance health services. Prescribing any treatment before a clinical examination of the patient is prohibited; the health authorities may set a system for providing distance (remote) health services. Quote: "Prescribe any treatment before carrying out the clinical examination of the patient.". Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 5(5).

metadata.themes: prescription, clinical examination, telehealth, remote consultation

text: No unnecessary procedures without informed consent. Performing unnecessary medical procedures or surgeries without the patient's informed consent is prohibited. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 5(10).

Definition of medical error. Defines medical error, the basis of a practitioner's liability. It addresses the practitioner's error; it does not allocate responsibility for an AI suggestion validated by the practitioner. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 6.

metadata.themes: liability, medical error, AI suggestion liability

text: Written consent for surgery. Written consent of the patient is required for surgical interventions. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 8(1)(c).

No abortion and no prescription that may cause abortion (limited exceptions). A doctor may neither perform an abortion nor prescribe anything that may cause abortion of a pregnant woman. Exceptions: (1) danger to the mother's life with no other means, decided by an obstetrician with the treating doctor and a written report signed by the spouses; (2) proven serious, incurable fetal deformity, with written consent of both spouses, within 120 days of pregnancy and confirmed by a medical committee. Quote: "A doctor may neither conduct any abortion operation nor prescribe anything that may cause the abortion". Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 16.

Disciplinary sanctions including licence suspension. Provides for disciplinary measures against practitioners, including suspension of the licence. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 23.
Mandatory civil liability insurance. Insurance against civil liability for medical errors is mandatory. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (4) of 2016 Concerning Medical Liability, Art. 25.

Confidentiality, integrity and availability of health data. When using ICT in health: (1) keep health data confidential and do not circulate it outside permitted cases; (2) ensure its validity and credibility by protecting it from unauthorised damage, amendment, alteration, deletion or addition; (3) ensure availability to authorised persons. Quote: "To ensure the validity and credibility of the health data and information". Source: Federal Law No. (2) of 2019 Concerning the Use of Information and Communication Technology in Health Fields, Art. 4.

metadata.themes: confidentiality, integrity, tamper-evident log, audit trail, availability

text: Health data may not be stored or processed outside the State. Health data relating to health services provided in the UAE may not be stored, processed, generated or transferred outside the State, except where a resolution is issued by the Health Authority in coordination with the Ministry. (MEDIMCOM interpretation, not the text: sending consultation content to a cloud AI service hosted abroad is processing outside the State.) Quote: "It is not permissible to store, process, generate or transform the health data and information outside State". Source: Federal Law No. (2) of 2019 Concerning the Use of Information and Communication Technology in Health Fields, Art. 13.

metadata.themes: data localisation, cross-border transfer, cloud AI, foreign server, outside UAE

text: Use of patient information only for health purposes without written approval. Patient information must be kept confidential and used only for health purposes without the patient's written approval, except: (1) insurers or funders reviewing entitlements; (2) scientific and clinical research without disclosing identity; (3) preventive and curative public-health measures or protecting the patient or contacts; (4) request of judicial authorities; (5) Health Authority request for monitoring, inspection and public health. Source: Federal Law No. (2) of 2019 Concerning the Use of Information and Communication Technology in Health Fields, Art. 16.

metadata.themes: confidentiality, secondary use, commercial use, written consent, research, public health, insurance, judicial request

text: Retention of health data for at least 25 years. Health data kept through ICT must be retained for a period commensurate with need and not less than 25 years from the last health procedure, with confidentiality, validity and credibility ensured. Source: Federal Law No. (2) of 2019 Concerning the Use of Information and Communication Technology in Health Fields, Art. 20(1).

Penalty for violating the localisation rule. Violating Article 13 is punishable by a fine of AED 500,000 to AED 700,000. Source: Federal Law No. (2) of 2019 Concerning the Use of Information and Communication Technology in Health Fields, Art. 24.

Exceptions allowing health data outside the UAE. Health data may be stored or transferred abroad in listed cases, including: treatment of the patient abroad; samples sent to foreign laboratories; scientific research under UAE rules; UAE insurers needing data abroad with patient consent; requests by cooperating competent authorities; simple personal medical devices; pharmacovigilance; and other cases approved by the health authorities. Source: Ministry of Health and Prevention Resolution No. (51) of 2021 on cases where health data may be stored or transferred outside the State, list of exceptions.

metadata.themes: data localisation exceptions, foreign laboratory, research, telemedicine, cross-border transfer

text: Conditions on permitted transfers. Permitted transfers remain subject to controls reported as: written patient consent, limits on sharing, encryption to best standards, and a copy of the data stored inside the country. Source: Ministry of Health and Prevention Resolution No. (51) of 2021 on cases where health data may be stored or transferred outside the State, conditions.

metadata.themes: data localisation exceptions, encryption, copy in UAE, written consent

text: Scope exclusions: government data and regulated health data. The decree-law does not apply to government data or to personal health data that has its own legislation regulating its protection and processing. Health data in MEDIMCOM is therefore governed first by Federal Law No. 2 of 2019. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data, Art. 2(2)(a),(e).

Right to object to automated decisions. A data subject may object to decisions based on automated processing, including profiling, that have legal or seriously adverse effects, unless the processing is agreed in a contract, required by law, or consented to in advance. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data, Art. 18.

metadata.themes: automated decision, human oversight, profiling, right to object

text: Cross-border transfer of (non-health) personal data. Transfers are allowed to countries with adequate protection or under agreements (Art. 22); otherwise under contractual safeguards or explicit consent where not contrary to public or security interests (Art. 23). Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data, Arts. 22-23.

AI-based products can be medical equipment. Medical Equipment is a medical product containing a substance, device, instrument, implant or system, including accessories and operating software, and includes wearable devices and products based on AI technology. Quote: "shall include wearable devices and products based on AI technology". Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments, Art. 1 (definition of Medical Equipment).

metadata.themes: software as medical device, AI medical device, regulatory status, SaMD

text: A prescription is issued by a licensed practitioner. A prescription is a document issued by a licensed practitioner to a practitioner authorised to dispense; verbal orders must later be documented as set by ministerial resolution. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments, Art. 1 (definition of Prescription).

Marketing approval required. Importing, distributing, selling, using or manufacturing medical products for circulation is prohibited without marketing approval from the Emirates Drug Establishment. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments, Art. 5(1).

metadata.themes: marketing authorisation, unregistered medicine, medicine approval

text: Emergency use approval. The decree-law provides for emergency use approval of medical products. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments, Arts. 11-13.

Prescribing only when authorised. Licensed health practitioners may not advise on, prescribe or dispense medical products unless authorised under the decree-law and its regulations. Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments, Art. 42(2).

Controlled products only on a licensed human physician's prescription. Pharmacists may dispense controlled products for patients only on a prescription from a licensed human physician (separate rules for veterinary use). Source: Federal Decree-Law No. (38) of 2024 Governing Medical Products, Pharmacists and Pharmaceutical Establishments, Art. 55.

Right to communicate and to information through sign language and other means. People of determination have the right to express themselves and to seek, receive and impart information on an equal footing, using Braille, sign language and other means of communication. Source: Federal Law No. (29) of 2006 Concerning the Rights of People with Special Needs (People of Determination), as amended by Federal Law No. (14) of 2009, Art. 7.

metadata.themes: accessible communication, sign language, pictograms, alternative communication, deaf

text: Health and rehabilitation services. People of determination are entitled to health and rehabilitation services, at the State's expense, as set out by the law. Source: Federal Law No. (29) of 2006 Concerning the Rights of People with Special Needs (People of Determination), as amended by Federal Law No. (14) of 2009, Art. 10.

Substitute means of communication. The law provides for substitute (alternative) means of communication for people of determination. Source: Federal Law No. (29) of 2006 Concerning the Rights of People with Special Needs (People of Determination), as amended by Federal Law No. (14) of 2009, Art. 13.

Simplified materials. Provides for simplified materials adapted to people of determination. Source: Federal Law No. (29) of 2006 Concerning the Rights of People with Special Needs (People of Determination), as amended by Federal Law No. (14) of 2009, Art. 20(2).

metadata.themes: easy read, simplified information, low literacy

text: Duty to notify communicable diseases. Physicians, pharmacists and other practitioners must notify their supervising body no later than 24 hours after knowing or suspecting a Group (A) disease listed in Schedule 1; other persons (contacts, supervisors, facility managers) must notify immediately. Source: Federal Law No. (14) of 2014 On Control of Communicable Diseases, Art. 4.

metadata.themes: notification, outbreak, 24 hours, reporting duty, epidemic

text: Notification by health bodies and facilities. The Ministry, health bodies and private health facilities must notify immediately and no later than 24 hours for Group (A) diseases and 7 days for Group (B) diseases. Source: Federal Law No. (14) of 2014 On Control of Communicable Diseases, Art. 5.

Immediate action and cooperation of health facilities. On notification, the Ministry and health body act immediately (isolation where needed, testing, referral); health facilities must fully cooperate by providing diagnosis, treatment and follow-up information. Source: Federal Law No. (14) of 2014 On Control of Communicable Diseases, Art. 10.

Powers during an epidemic. During an epidemic the Ministry and health body, with the concerned bodies, may declare an infected area, regulate entry and exit, restrict gatherings, regulate public places and apply measures to patients, suspects and contacts. Source: Federal Law No. (14) of 2014 On Control of Communicable Diseases, Art. 18.

Confidentiality of infected persons' information. Infected persons are entitled to confidentiality of their disease-related information, which may be disclosed only in cases prescribed by law. Source: Federal Law No. (14) of 2014 On Control of Communicable Diseases, Art. 29.

metadata.themes: confidentiality, outbreak, data sharing in crisis

text: AI supports; a human decides. AI in healthcare is treated as supportive technology: it requires a human to make final decisions and be responsible for any actions taken by the technology. Quote: "it requires a human to make final decisions and be responsible for any actions taken by the technology". Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Policy on Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare Sector (Policy/AI/0.9), Policy statement (AI as supportive technology).

metadata.themes: human oversight, final decision, supportive technology, AI suggestion

text: Verifiable and explainable AI; developers accountable. AI software should be verifiable and explainable; developers are accountable; major versions require certification and re-certification; validation must be auditable; regular audits and feedback to DoH. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Policy on Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare Sector (Policy/AI/0.9), Policy statement (verifiable and explainable).

Graceful degradation. AI solutions should degrade gracefully when components fail, so that care continues safely. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Policy on Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare Sector (Policy/AI/0.9), Policy statement (graceful degradation).

Clinicians keep ultimate decision-making authority. Clinicians should retain ultimate decision-making authority in all AI-assisted healthcare scenarios. Quote: "Clinicians should retain ultimate decision-making authority in all AI-assisted healthcare scenarios.". Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.7.2.2.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025
metadata.themes: human oversight, final decision, clinician authority, AI suggestion

text: Inform patients when AI contributes to decisions. Systems must include mechanisms to inform patients when AI contributes to clinical or operational decisions, including its function, limitations and intended outcomes. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.6.1.1.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025

text: Consent mechanisms and opt-out for AI-driven services. Clear consent mechanisms must ensure informed decision-making and transparency; patients are told they can opt out of AI-driven services where applicable. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.6.1.3.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025

text: All decisions logged and traceable. All decisions, changes, updates and interventions must be logged and traceable to a responsible party. Quote: "All decisions, changes, updates, and interventions must be logged and traceable to a responsible party.". Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.7.1.3.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025

text: Report adverse outcomes and ethical concerns. Governance includes reporting adverse outcomes or ethical concerns to governance bodies. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.7.1.2.3.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025

text: Compute and storage in the UAE. Compute and storage infrastructure, including disaster-recovery sites, must be located in the UAE; remote access for development and support teams should be exclusively from within the UAE. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.4.5.1.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025
metadata.themes: data localisation, cloud AI, hosting, outside UAE

text: Datasets reflect population diversity. All training, validation and test datasets must reflect the diversity of the target population. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.5.1.1.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025

text: Validation before deployment. AI models shall undergo rigorous validation against established performance benchmarks before deployment. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.1.3.1.1.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025

text: Risk classes: very high risk prohibited, high risk assessed. AI systems with very high residual risk must be prohibited from deployment; high-risk systems require conformity assessments before and after deployment. Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI) Standard (DoH/ST/DDGO/RAI/V1/2025), Sec. 3.3.1.2.2.

metadata.source_title: DoH Abu Dhabi Responsible AI Standard 2025

text: Supportive technology needs a human final decision. Supportive technology requires a human to make final decisions and be responsible for any actions taken by the technology. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Definitions (Supportive Technology).

metadata.themes: human oversight, final decision, supportive technology

text: Accountability and appeals. Accountability for outcomes of an AI solution must be agreed; developers are accountable to end users; solutions must have built-in appeal procedures so users can challenge significant decisions. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Sec. 4.2.1-4.2.3.

metadata.themes: accountability, liability, appeal, AI suggestion liability

text: Failures traced, diagnosed and controlled. Developers must build systems whose failures can be traced, diagnosed and controlled. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Sec. 4.3.1.

Mandatory disclosure, including the professional's role. AI solutions must disclose, among other items, their AI-enabled functions, validation, data sets, algorithm type, the role of the healthcare professional in the final decision and the limitations of data and algorithms. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Sec. 4.3.2.

Independent third-party validation. All AI solutions for healthcare must undergo independent validation by a competent third party. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Sec. 4.3.3.

Supervised by end users; can be overridden. AI solutions must be safe, secure and supervised by end users, and must be able to be overridden or their decisions reversed by designated end users. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Sec. 4.4.1-4.4.2.

metadata.themes: human oversight, override, validation by doctor

text: Auditable validation statements. AI tools must include auditable validation statements. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Sec. 4.6.12.

Incident reporting and independent audits. Adverse events should be reported in a timely way to oversight bodies; all known or suspected AI incidents or deficiencies, and issues that may affect patient safety, are reported to DHA; regular independent audits are conducted. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Policy: Artificial Intelligence in the Healthcare (DHA/HISHD/PP-09), Sec. 4.6.17, 4.8.1-4.8.2, 4.8.5.

No narcotic, controlled or semi-controlled medicines via telehealth. The physician shall not prescribe narcotic, controlled or semi-controlled medication through telehealth services. Quote: "The physician shall not prescribe Narcotic, Controlled or Semi-controlled medication through telehealth services.". Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 17.12.7 (also 4.2.2, 17.3.1(e)).

metadata.themes: telehealth, remote prescription, controlled medicine, narcotics

text: Telehealth prescriptions follow the MOHAP drug list and an online prescription system. Prescribing via telehealth follows the UAE MOHAP drug list, and prescriptions must be issued through an online prescription system with electronic transfer. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 17.12.6, 17.13.1(d).

Telehealth consent documented at each encounter. The professional obtains and documents consent from the patient or guardian; electronic consent is acceptable; consent for treatment must be documented at each encounter. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 10.1, 10.1.1, 10.4.2.

Patient identification with at least three identifiers. The patient is identified with at least three identifiers (e.g. full name, date of birth, Emirates ID, record number, phone), and identity is verified and consent granted before diagnosis. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 10.2.1, 14.5.5.

Documentation and 25-year retention. All telehealth encounters are documented in the medical record (service type, participants' licence numbers, locations, confirmation of consent) and retained for at least 25 years. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 11.4, 11.6, 11.10.

Telehealth data stays in the UAE. Telehealth data is stored with a cloud service provider in the UAE; storing, developing or transferring health data outside the country is not permitted unless applicable law allows. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 7.6.7, 8.2.5(d), 10.6.4.

metadata.themes: data localisation, cloud AI, outside UAE

text: People of determination and understandable language. Provisions must be in place for People of Determination and access must not exclude them; consultations are offered at least in Arabic and English, interpretation services are encouraged, and information is given in a language the patient easily understands. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 14.1.5(a), 8.3.5, 14.1.6, 9.6.3.

metadata.themes: accessible communication, people of determination, deaf, interpretation, pictograms

text: Emergency protocols in telehealth. Providers must have tested written protocols for emergency requests, emergency contact numbers, and must not delay advice to seek emergency services. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 12.4-12.4.3, 14.1.4(c).

Explain limits of prescribing without tests. Limitations of prescribing without confirmatory laboratory testing must be explained to the patient. Source: Dubai Health Authority - Standards for Telehealth Services (DHA/HRS/HPSD/ST-14, version 4), Sec. 9.8.2.

Abu Dhabi tele-medicine services. The DOH Standard on Tele-Medicine (effective 16 September 2020) covers tele-diagnosis, tele-counseling, tele-medical interventions, tele-consultation, tele-prescription and tele-monitoring, and applies to DOH-licensed or approved facilities. Quote: "Healthcare facilities licensed or approved by DOH to provide tele-medicine services.". Source: Department of Health Abu Dhabi - Standard on Tele-Medicine, Sections 1-2.

Human oversight. The Charter affirms the irreplaceable value of human judgment and human oversight over AI. Source: The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, Principle 6.

Data privacy and transparency. Privacy of community members is a top priority, and AI systems should be understandable in how they operate and decide. Source: The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, Principles 4-5.

Inclusive access and compliance with treaties and laws. AI awareness for an inclusive future (equitable access for all segments of society) and commitment to international treaties and local laws. Source: The UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence, Principles 11-12.

Healthcare is a priority sector; strong governance. The strategy names healthcare among priority sectors and sets objectives including providing data and infrastructure to become an AI test bed (7) and ensuring strong governance and effective regulation (8). Source: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031, Strategic objectives 2, 7, 8; priority sectors.

metadata.themes: national strategy, healthcare, governance, sandbox, test bed

text: UAE is a State Party to the CRPD. The UAE signed the CRPD on 12 February 2008 and ratified it (Presidential Decree of 24 December 2009); the report's introduction refers to 19 March 2010. Source: Initial report of the United Arab Emirates to the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD/C/ARE/1), Paras. 3, 66-67.

metadata.source_title: UAE report to the CRPD Committee

text: Accessible information and alternative communication. States provide public information in accessible formats in a timely manner at no extra cost; accept and facilitate sign languages, Braille, augmentative and alternative communication and other accessible means chosen by persons with disabilities in official interactions; recognise and promote sign languages. Quote: "Accepting and facilitating the use of sign languages, Braille, augmentative and alternative communication,". Source: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Art. 21(a)-(b),(e).

metadata.jurisdiction: International (binding on the UAE and Cameroon as States Parties)
metadata.themes: accessible communication, augmentative and alternative communication, pictograms, sign language, deaf

text: Accessibility of information and communication. Accessibility applies to the physical environment and to information and communications, including technologies and systems. Source: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Art. 9.

metadata.jurisdiction: International (binding on the UAE and Cameroon as States Parties)

text: Situations of risk and humanitarian emergencies. States take all necessary measures to protect persons with disabilities in situations of risk, including armed conflict, humanitarian emergencies and natural disasters. Source: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Art. 11.

metadata.jurisdiction: International (binding on the UAE and Cameroon as States Parties)

text: Legal capacity and support in exercising it. Persons with disabilities enjoy legal capacity on an equal basis, and States provide access to the support they may require in exercising it (relevant to consent given through alternative communication). Source: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Art. 12.

metadata.jurisdiction: International (binding on the UAE and Cameroon as States Parties)
metadata.themes: legal capacity, supported decision-making, consent, pictograms

text: Right to health; care on the basis of free and informed consent. Persons with disabilities have the right to the highest attainable standard of health without discrimination; health professionals provide care of the same quality on the basis of free and informed consent. Source: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, Art. 25.

metadata.jurisdiction: International (binding on the UAE and Cameroon as States Parties)

text: Notify WHO within 24 hours. Each State Party notifies WHO, through its National IHR Focal Point, within 24 hours of assessment of events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern. Source: International Health Regulations (2005), Art. 6(1).

Confidentiality of personal health information under the IHR. Health information about identifiable persons collected or received under the IHR is kept confidential and processed anonymously as required by national law. Quote: "which refers to an identified or identifiable person shall be kept confidential". Source: International Health Regulations (2005), Art. 45(1).

WHO principles for AI in health. Protect human autonomy; promote human well-being, safety and the public interest; ensure transparency, explainability and intelligibility; foster responsibility and accountability; ensure inclusiveness and equity; promote AI that is responsive and sustainable. Source: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: WHO guidance, Six guiding principles.

Governance of large multi-modal models in health. Governments should assign a regulator to assess and approve LMMs for health use, and require independent post-release audits and impact assessments, with results disaggregated by user characteristics such as disability. Source: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: Guidance on large multi-modal models, Key recommendations.

Human oversight and determination. Principle of human oversight and determination: humans may rely on AI for efficiency, but an AI system can never replace ultimate human responsibility and accountability. Quote: "an AI system can never replace ultimate human responsibility and accountability". Source: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, Para. 36.

Automatic logging over the lifetime. High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over their lifetime, to detect risks and substantial modifications and support post-market monitoring. Quote: "High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.". Source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), Art. 12.

Human oversight, including awareness of automation bias. High-risk AI systems are designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them, prevent or minimise risks to health, safety and fundamental rights, remain aware of automation bias, and decide not to use or to override the output. Source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), Art. 14.

AI regulatory sandboxes and use of personal data in them. Member States set up AI regulatory sandboxes; personal data lawfully collected for other purposes may be used in a sandbox only for substantial public interest (including public health), when anonymised or synthetic data cannot meet the need, in an isolated environment, with logs, no effects on data subjects and deletion at the end. Source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), Arts. 57-59.

metadata.themes: regulatory sandbox, synthetic data, data localisation, innovation

text: Reporting serious incidents. Providers of high-risk AI systems report serious incidents to market surveillance authorities immediately once a causal link is established or reasonably likely, and no later than 15 days after becoming aware (shorter limits for widespread or fatal incidents). Source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), Art. 73.

Software is a product; disclosure and presumption of defect. Software, including AI and software-as-a-service, is a product for strict liability; courts can order disclosure of evidence (Art. 9) and presume defectiveness when evidence is not disclosed or safety requirements are breached (Art. 10). Quote: "includes electricity, digital manufacturing files, raw materials and software". Source: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on liability for defective products, Arts. 4, 9, 10.

metadata.themes: liability, software liability, AI suggestion liability

text: Decision-support software classified at least class IIa. Software intended to provide information used to take decisions with diagnostic or therapeutic purposes is at least class IIa (higher if decisions may cause serious harm or death). Source: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices - Annex VIII, Rule 11, Annex VIII, Rule 11.

metadata.themes: software as medical device, classification, regulatory status

text: Equivalent access to emergency services for persons with disabilities. Member States ensure that end-users with disabilities have access to emergency services through emergency communications equivalent to that enjoyed by other end-users. Source: Directive (EU) 2018/1972 establishing the European Electronic Communications Code - Article 109, Art. 109(5).

When decision-support software is not a device. Software is non-device clinical decision support when it (1) does not analyse medical images or signals, (2) displays or analyses medical information, (3) supports a health professional's recommendations, and (4) lets the professional independently review the basis of recommendations without relying primarily on them; the 2026 revision places automation-bias concerns under criterion 4. Source: FDA guidance: Clinical Decision Support Software (revised final guidance), Four non-device criteria.

metadata.themes: software as medical device, regulatory status, automation bias, explainability

text: Avoid NSAIDs from 20 weeks of pregnancy. Avoid NSAIDs at 20 weeks or later in pregnancy unless specifically advised by a health professional; does not apply to low-dose aspirin; other medicines such as acetaminophen (paracetamol) are available for pain and fever. Quote: "Other medicines, such as acetaminophen, are available to treat pain and fever during pregnancy.". Source: FDA Drug Safety Communication: avoid use of NSAIDs in pregnancy at 20 weeks or later, Recommendation.

Misoprostol can cause abortion. Misoprostol administered to pregnant women can cause birth defects, abortion, premature birth or uterine rupture; patients must be advised of its abortifacient property. Quote: "CAN CAUSE BIRTH DEFECTS, ABORTION, PREMATURE BIRTH OR UTERINE RUPTURE.". Source: CYTOTEC (misoprostol) prescribing information - Boxed Warning, Boxed warning.

Identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs. Since 1 August 2016, organisations providing NHS or publicly funded adult social care must identify, record, flag, share and meet the information and communication support needs of people with a disability, impairment or sensory loss. Source: NHS England - Accessible Information Standard (DCB1605), Standard DCB1605.

metadata.themes: accessible communication, deaf, communication needs, health records

text: Regulatory sandbox for AI medical devices. A regulatory sandbox pilot launched in 2024 to identify and address challenges of regulating standalone AI medical devices used in NHS settings, informing future guidance. Source: MHRA AI Airlock - regulatory sandbox for AI as a Medical Device, Programme description.

metadata.themes: regulatory sandbox, AI medical device, innovation

text: Testing comprehension of graphical symbols. Specifies a method of testing what proportion of people comprehend a graphical symbol correctly, used to choose the most comprehensible variant. Source: ISO 9186-1:2014 Graphical symbols - Test methods - Part 1: Method for testing comprehensibility, Scope (Introduction).

metadata.themes: pictograms, comprehension testing, validation of pictograms

text: ML pipeline architecture. Defines an architectural framework for machine learning in future networks, including an ML pipeline and ML management and orchestration functions, and how to integrate them. Source: ITU-T Recommendation Y.3172 (06/2019) Architectural framework for machine learning in future networks including IMT-2020, Summary.

ITU AI readiness factors. Preliminary readiness factors: data, research, deployment support, standards, open source and code, sandbox environments. Source: ITU AI for Good - Preliminary Analysis Towards a Standardized Readiness Framework, Readiness factors.

AI readiness factors (Report 2.0). Six readiness factors: data (availability and quality of datasets), research (collaboration between domain and AI research), deployment support (physical, communication and backend infrastructure), standards (trust, interoperability, compliance), open source and code, sandbox environments for experimentation and validation. Source: AI Ready – Analysis Towards a Standardized Readiness Framework, Report 2.0, Factors.

metadata.themes: AI readiness, ITU, sandbox, open source

text: Human interface. Ease of human interaction with AI systems; metrics include AI-supported interfaces and interaction channels, local-language model availability, usability, cultural sensitivity and safety safeguards. Source: AI Ready – Analysis Towards a Standardized Readiness Framework, Report 2.0, Dimension 6.

metadata.themes: AI readiness, accessibility, human interface, local language

text: Collaboration with AI. Human-AI co-creation and shared decision-making; metrics include feedback loops, trust metrics and comparison of co-created output with human-only or AI-only baselines. Source: AI Ready – Analysis Towards a Standardized Readiness Framework, Report 2.0, Dimension 8.

metadata.themes: AI readiness, human oversight, shared decision

text: AI and policies. Testing policies in sandboxes and ensuring policies enable AI integration; metrics include vertical sandboxes and domain-specific policy evaluation, simulation of policy impacts, horizontal policies on data, AI lifecycle and explainability, policy briefs, audits and data sovereignty. Source: AI Ready – Analysis Towards a Standardized Readiness Framework, Report 2.0, Dimension 10.

metadata.themes: AI readiness, policy, sandbox, data sovereignty, audit

text: AI for inclusion. Using AI to bridge social divides, including accessibility; metrics include edge AI with privacy and low latency, generative AI support for sign languages and regional languages, offline kits and number of beneficiaries. Source: AI Ready – Analysis Towards a Standardized Readiness Framework, Report 2.0, Dimension 11.

metadata.themes: AI readiness, inclusion, accessibility, sign language, deaf

text: African Union continental AI strategy. Endorsed in July 2024; promotes ethical, responsible and equitable AI, unified national approaches and inclusive AI development; names healthcare among sectors transformed by AI. Source: African Union - Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy, Strategy summary.

Cameroon: practice of medicine reserved to registered physicians (comparative). Cameroon's 1990 law organises the medical profession (registration with the Order of Physicians); article-level content to be re-read before citation. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 90/36 du 10 août 1990 relative à l'exercice et à l'organisation de la profession de médecin, Document level.

Cameroon: personal data protection law applicable from 23 June 2026 (comparative). Cameroon's 2024 personal data law, applicable from 23 June 2026, regulates processing and cross-border transfers; article-level content to be re-read before citation. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2024/017 du 23 décembre 2024 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, Document level.

Practice of medicine reserved to physicians registered with the Order. No one may practise medicine in Cameroon unless registered on the roll of the Ordre national des médecins. Quote: "Nul ne peut exercer la profession de médecin au Cameroun s'il n'est pas inscrit au tableau de l'Ordre.". Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 90/36 du 10 août 1990 relative à l'exercice et à l'organisation de la profession de médecin, Art. 2(1).

Physicians bound by professional secrecy. A physician practising in public administration or the private sector is bound by professional secrecy (scope defined elsewhere). Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 90/36 du 10 août 1990 relative à l'exercice et à l'organisation de la profession de médecin, Art. 4.

Illegal practice of medicine and penalties. Illegal practice includes an unauthorised person habitually taking part in diagnosis or treatment, even in a doctor's presence; penalties: 6 days to 6 months' imprisonment and/or a fine of 200,000 to 2,000,000 FCFA, with immediate cessation. Quote: "à l'établissement de diagnostics ou aux traitements d'affections par actes professionnels". Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 90/36 du 10 août 1990 relative à l'exercice et à l'organisation de la profession de médecin, Art. 16-17.

metadata.themes: illegal practice, diagnosis, treatment, AI, Cameroon

text: Consent to personal data processing. Consent to processing must be free, informed, specific, unambiguous and express, obtained before processing; parental consent for minors under 18. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2024/017 du 23 décembre 2024 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, Art. 9 (secondary).

Health data are sensitive data. Sensitive data, including health data, may in principle not be processed, except on listed legal bases such as the protection of health. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2024/017 du 23 décembre 2024 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, sensitive data (article to confirm).

metadata.themes: health data, sensitive data, processing, Cameroon

text: Transfers of personal data outside Cameroon. Transfers of personal data to another country require appropriate safeguards and, according to secondary sources, prior authorisation of the data protection authority. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2024/017 du 23 décembre 2024 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, transfers abroad (article to confirm).

metadata.themes: cross-border transfer, data localisation, foreign cloud AI, Cameroon

text: Personal data protection authority. Creates an independent data protection authority; its organisation is to be set by presidential decree. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2024/017 du 23 décembre 2024 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, Art. 53 (secondary).

Sanctions for breaches. Administrative fines up to 1 billion FCFA for the most serious breaches; criminal sanctions also apply (unauthorised processing, illegal transfers). Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2024/017 du 23 décembre 2024 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, Art. 70 (secondary).

Compliance deadline. Data controllers had 18 months from promulgation (23 December 2024), i.e. until 23 June 2026, to comply. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2024/017 du 23 décembre 2024 relative à la protection des données à caractère personnel, Art. 73 (secondary).

Deaf persons are persons with a sensory disability. Sensory disabilities include deaf, deaf-mute, mute and hard-of-hearing persons. Quote: "sourds, sourds - muets, muets, malentendants". Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2010/002 du 13 avril 2010 portant protection et promotion des personnes handicapées, Art. 3.

State coverage of health care for eligible persons with disabilities. Indigent persons holding a national disability card receive total or partial State coverage of rehabilitation, consultations, laboratory tests, imaging, hospitalisation, evacuations and some medicines. Quote: "une prise en charge totale ou partielle par l'état". Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2010/002 du 13 avril 2010 portant protection et promotion des personnes handicapées, Art. 22.

Access of persons with disabilities to information technologies. The State, decentralised authorities and civil society must facilitate access of persons with disabilities to information technologies. Quote: "L'accès des personnes handicapées aux technologies de l'information". Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2010/002 du 13 avril 2010 portant protection et promotion des personnes handicapées, Art. 32.

Medical ethics: consent, information, prescription, secrecy. The code of medical ethics governs consent to care, information of the patient, written prescriptions and medical secrecy; article numbers to be read before citation. Source: Cameroun - Décret n° 83/166 du 12 avril 1983 portant code de déontologie médicale, Document level (articles to confirm).

metadata.themes: consent, patient information, prescription, medical secrecy, Cameroon

text: Pharmacy and medicines. Organises the pharmacy profession; marketing authorisation of medicines to be checked with the national regulator. Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 90/035 du 10 août 1990 relative à l'exercice et à l'organisation de la profession de pharmacien, Document level (to read).

Criminal sanction of breaches of professional secrecy. According to legal doctrine, breaches of medical secrecy are punished under Article 310 of the Penal Code (penalty not read). Source: Cameroun - Loi n° 2016/007 du 12 juillet 2016 portant Code pénal (secret professionnel), Art. 310 (doctrine).

Tramadol in pregnancy: neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Prolonged use of tramadol during pregnancy can result in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognised and treated; the prescriber should weigh this risk and inform the patient. Quote: "Prolonged use of tramadol hydrochloride during pregnancy can result in neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome". Source: Tramadol hydrochloride tablets — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 3/2021, Boxed warning; 5.4.

Tramadol in children and adolescents. Tramadol is contraindicated in all children younger than 12 years and after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy in children younger than 18; its use should be avoided in adolescents 12 to 18 years who have other risk factors. Quote: "Avoid the use of tramadol hydrochloride in adolescents 12 to 18 years of age who have other risk factors". Source: Tramadol hydrochloride tablets — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 3/2021, Contraindications 4; Warnings 5.5.

Tramadol maximum daily dose. Tramadol tablets must not be given at a dose exceeding 400 mg per day. Quote: "Do not administer tramadol hydrochloride tablets at a dose exceeding 400 mg per day.". Source: Tramadol hydrochloride tablets — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 3/2021, Dosage and administration 2.

Metformin maximum daily dose. Adults: up to a maximum of 2550 mg per day in divided doses; paediatric patients (10 years and older): up to 2000 mg per day. Quote: "up to a maximum dose of 2550 mg per day, given in divided doses.". Source: Metformin hydrochloride tablets — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 6/2026, 2.1, 2.2.

Metformin and renal impairment. Metformin is contraindicated in severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2); starting it at an eGFR between 30 and 45 is not recommended; renal function must be assessed before initiation. Quote: "Severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2)". Source: Metformin hydrochloride tablets — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 6/2026, 2.3; 4.

metadata.themes: renal impairment, kidney, metformin, lactic acidosis

text: Metformin and hepatic impairment. Metformin is not recommended in patients with hepatic impairment (risk of lactic acidosis). Quote: "Metformin Hydrochloride Tablets are not recommended in patients with hepatic impairment.". Source: Metformin hydrochloride tablets — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 6/2026, 8.7.

Amoxicillin and beta-lactam hypersensitivity. Amoxicillin is contraindicated in patients who have had a serious hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin or to other beta-lactam antibacterials (penicillins, cephalosporins). Quote: "contraindicated in patients who have experienced a serious hypersensitivity reaction". Source: Amoxicillin capsules — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 01/2024, 4.

Amoxicillin and severe renal impairment. No dose reduction unless renal impairment is severe; patients with a glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min should not receive the 875 mg dose. Quote: "Renal impairment patients with a glomerular filtration rate of less than 30 mL/min should NOT receive the 875 mg dose.". Source: Amoxicillin capsules — FDA-approved prescribing information (DailyMed), revised 01/2024, 2.3.

Acetaminophen: liver warning and maximum daily dose. Severe liver damage may occur above 4,000 mg of acetaminophen in 24 hours, with other acetaminophen-containing drugs, or with 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day; ask a doctor before use in liver disease and a doctor or pharmacist when taking warfarin. Quote: "more than 4,000 mg of acetaminophen in 24 hours". Source: Acetaminophen 500 mg tablets — FDA OTC Drug Facts label (reproduced by NDC List), Drug Facts: Warnings.

metadata.themes: paracetamol, acetaminophen, liver, maximum dose, warfarin

text: Ibuprofen: stomach bleeding and conditions needing a doctor's advice. Stomach bleeding risk is higher at age 60 or older, with past stomach ulcers or bleeding problems, or when taking a blood thinning (anticoagulant) or steroid drug; ask a doctor before use with high blood pressure, heart disease, liver cirrhosis, kidney disease, asthma or past stroke. Quote: "take a blood thinning (anticoagulant) or steroid drug". Source: Ibuprofen 200 mg tablets — FDA OTC Drug Facts label (reproduced by NDC List), Drug Facts: Warnings.

metadata.themes: ibuprofen, NSAID, bleeding, ulcer, anticoagulant, kidney, heart

text: Ibuprofen: last 3 months of pregnancy. It is especially important not to use ibuprofen during the last 3 months of pregnancy unless definitely directed by a doctor. Quote: "It is especially important not to use ibuprofen during the last 3 months of pregnancy". Source: Ibuprofen 200 mg tablets — FDA OTC Drug Facts label (reproduced by NDC List), Drug Facts: Warnings.

Ibuprofen maximum daily dose (prescription). Prescription ibuprofen: do not exceed 3200 mg total daily dose. Quote: "Do not exceed 3200 mg total daily dose.". Source: Ibuprofen tablets USP — prescription label (reproduced by MedLibrary), Dosage and administration.

Aspirin: Reye's syndrome in children and teenagers. Children and teenagers who have or are recovering from chicken pox or flu-like symptoms should not use aspirin (Reye's syndrome, rare but serious). Quote: "Children and teenagers who have or are recovering from chicken pox or flu-like symptoms should not use this product.". Source: Aspirin 325 mg tablets — FDA OTC Drug Facts label (reproduced by NDC List), Drug Facts: Warnings.

Aspirin: last 3 months of pregnancy. It is especially important not to use aspirin during the last 3 months of pregnancy unless definitely directed by a doctor. Quote: "It is especially important not to use aspirin during the last 3 months of pregnancy.". Source: Aspirin 325 mg tablets — FDA OTC Drug Facts label (reproduced by NDC List), Drug Facts: Warnings.

Aspirin: stomach bleeding and maximum daily dose. Stomach bleeding risk is higher with past stomach ulcers or bleeding problems or when taking a blood thinning (anticoagulant) or steroid drug; adults: no more than 12 tablets of 325 mg in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor. Quote: "do not take more than 12 tablets in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor". Source: Aspirin 325 mg tablets — FDA OTC Drug Facts label (reproduced by NDC List), Drug Facts: Warnings.

Policy gap L01 (Liability and accountability): Who answers for an AI suggestion that a clinician validated?. Situation: The assistant agent proposes an alternative treatment; the doctor accepts it; it later proves wrong. Missing: No binding rule allocating liability between clinician, software developer and facility when a validated AI suggestion causes harm, and no rule on the evidential value of AI logs in a dispute. MEDIMCOM response: Every AI suggestion carries its author agent, sources and status; overriding an A_REVOIR verdict requires a named doctor; the hash-chained journal can be produced as evidence.

Policy gap L02 (Regulatory status of software): When is a decision-support or communication assistant a medical device?. Situation: MEDIMCOM translates, suggests and checks; none of its agents prescribes, but its outputs influence decisions. Missing: The decree-law text read does not set criteria separating regulated decision-support software from non-device tools (communication aids, compliance checkers); executive regulations or EDE guidance on software to be checked. MEDIMCOM response: Designed to meet the 'reviewable basis' test: every suggestion and verdict shows its source text; the doctor decides.

Policy gap L03 (Accessible health communication): No operational standard for meeting deaf patients' communication needs in care. Situation: A deaf patient with limited literacy consults without a sign-language interpreter. Missing: No federal operational standard requiring providers to identify, record and flag a patient's communication need, nor rules on which alternative means (pictograms, easy-read, sign avatars) are acceptable in a clinical encounter. MEDIMCOM response: The communication need is stored in the patient state and travels with the record; the translator agent adapts every message; the doctor validates each pictogram sequence.

Policy gap L04 (Informed consent): Is consent given through pictograms valid informed consent?. Situation: The patient agrees to a treatment by selecting pictograms. Missing: No provision recognises consent expressed through augmentative and alternative communication, defines how comprehension is checked, or how such consent is documented. MEDIMCOM response: Consent is recorded with its means of expression, a comprehension check (teach-back with pictograms) and the doctor's attestation, all in the journal.

Policy gap L05 (Standards): No validation standard for medical pictograms. Situation: Pictograms are generated or chosen by a model and shown to patients. Missing: No UAE standard found on testing the comprehensibility of health pictograms or of AI-generated images used to inform patients. MEDIMCOM response: Pictogram library tested with deaf users following the ISO 9186-1 method before use; every sequence validated by the doctor.

Policy gap L06 (Data governance and innovation): Strict health-data localisation versus cloud AI and international sandboxes. Situation: A model or vector store hosted outside the UAE (e.g. an international sandbox) would process consultation content. Missing: No explicit pathway for AI testing in cross-border or international sandboxes, and no statement on whether synthetic or de-identified data falls outside the localisation rule. MEDIMCOM response: Local models only; synthetic data in the prototype; the jurist blocks any outbound transfer without an exception and its conditions.

Policy gap L07 (Human oversight and traceability): Oversight rules do not address multi-agent systems. Situation: Several AI agents exchange messages and act on a shared record before a human sees the result. Missing: No requirement on agent-to-agent communication, limits of agent autonomy, tool permissions, or tamper-evident logs. MEDIMCOM response: Typed messages between agents, per-agent tool permissions, deterministic verdicts, SHA-256 chained journal.

Policy gap L08 (Crisis coordination): No unified channel for AI incidents in health across emirates. Situation: During a crisis an AI component fails or gives harmful output in several facilities. Missing: Incident reporting duties are emirate-specific; no federal time limit or shared format for AI incidents found in the knowledge base. MEDIMCOM response: The journal exports an incident record (what, when, which agent, which sources); the jurist reminds the time limits that do exist.

Policy gap L09 (Accessible emergency communication): Emergency protocols do not guarantee equivalent access for deaf people. Situation: In an emergency the usual voice channels and interpreters are unavailable. Missing: No requirement found that health emergency protocols provide equivalent non-voice access for deaf patients. MEDIMCOM response: Emergency pictogram set always available offline; urgent alerts are prioritised by the assistant agent.
